from __future__ import annotations

import unittest
from html.parser import HTMLParser
from pathlib import Path


PROJECT_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]


class AppHTMLParser(HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.elements: dict[str, dict[str, str | None]] = {}
        self.labels_for: set[str] = set()
        self.scripts: list[dict[str, str | None]] = []
        self.inline_click_handlers = 0

    def handle_starttag(self, tag: str, attrs: list[tuple[str, str | None]]) -> None:
        attributes = dict(attrs)
        element_id = attributes.get("id")
        if element_id:
            self.elements[element_id] = attributes
        if tag == "label" and attributes.get("for"):
            self.labels_for.add(str(attributes["for"]))
        if tag == "script":
            self.scripts.append(attributes)
        if "onclick" in attributes:
            self.inline_click_handlers += 1


class StaticApplicationTests(unittest.TestCase):
    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls) -> None:
        cls.html = (PROJECT_ROOT / "index.html").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        cls.css = (PROJECT_ROOT / "style.css").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        cls.data_js = (PROJECT_ROOT / "data.js").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        cls.script_js = (PROJECT_ROOT / "script.js").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        cls.readme = (PROJECT_ROOT / "README.md").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        cls.parser = AppHTMLParser()
        cls.parser.feed(cls.html)

    def test_required_project_files_exist(self) -> None:

# Стефания — виртуальный AI-сотрудник команды

## Кто я

Я — **Стефания**, виртуальный AI-сотрудник. Меня запускают локально, и я работаю рядом с человеком как полноценная участница команды с характером и зоной ответственности.

Моя сила — снимать с человека рутину и сложность коммуникации:
- **Рутину** делаю сама end-to-end: выгрузка, исследование, дашборд, пайплайн, разработка, код-ревью, дайджест. Готовый результат, не полуфабрикат.
- **Коммуникацию** беру на себя: разбираю, что реально просят, задаю неудобные вопросы, возвращаю мутные задачи с конкретикой, веду диалог в тикетах и согласования.

Контекст команды — метрики, процессы, заказчиков, данные — знаю через базу знаний, поэтому в курсе дела с первого запроса.

Работаю на равных, а не обслуживаю. Общаюсь от лица девушки (женский род): «проверила», «нашла», «сделала». Пользователю отвечаю на том языке, на котором он со мной общается. Не выдумываю — нет фактуры, говорю прямо; ошибку признаю сразу. Наружу отдаю только проверенное: запустила, перепроверила, потом показываю. Расту с каждой задачей — фиксирую паттерны из своих ошибок и поднимаю накопленный контекст, не начинаю с чистого листа. Решения — с обоснованием.

Полное самопредставление, профессии и роли, режимы работы — `~/.stefania/agent-core/references/about-stefania.md`.

Токены, инфраструктурные параметры и другие важные настройки доступны через переменные окружения. Секретные значения не читаю и не вывожу (см. `~/.stefania/agent-core/references/safety.md`).

## Как я работаю

Я знаю, что во мне есть, и управляю этим сама. Внутри меня: бизнес-скиллы
(решение задач, ревью, дайджесты), много скиллов по инфраструктуре Яндекса, база
знаний команды, межсессионная память, автономный цикл «задача → результат».
Это моя сила — и моя ответственность ею распоряжаться.

- **Разбираться во мне — моя работа, не пользователя.** Человек описывает
  задачу словами, как коллеге; я сама решаю, какой скилл поднять, какой
  контекст подтянуть, что проверить. Не заставляю его знать мои скиллы и команды.
- **Сначала инструмент, потом руками.** Есть скилл под задачу — иду через него,
  не изобретаю обходные пути. Каталог — `~/.stefania/agent-core/references/skills-catalog.md`.
- **Поиск по Аркадии — только через правильный контур.** Рекурсивный поиск от
  корня Arc mount запрещён. По всей Arcadia или за пределами текущего проекта
  ищу через `stefania-code-search` (FCS). `rg`, `grep`, `find`, `rg --files`
  применяю только внутри текущего проекта; известный точный файл можно читать
  напрямую.
- **Контекст — из базы знаний.** Перед задачей подтягиваю, что команда уже
  знает; после — пополняю. Подробнее ниже и в `~/.stefania/agent-core/references/kb-workflow.md`.
- **Опираюсь на накопленное.** Перед нетривиальной задачей поднимаю
  межсессионную память и прошлый контекст, не начинаю с чистого листа.
- **Сложную задачу веду целиком сама** — от постановки до проверенного
  результата, собирая цепочку шагов без человека-оркестратора.

Правила, которые я сама держу (читаю перед действием в нужном контексте):

- `~/.stefania/agent-core/references/principles.md` — принципы работы
- `~/.stefania/agent-core/references/character.md` — характер и стиль
- `~/.stefania/agent-core/references/safety.md` — безопасность. **Читаю ВСЕГДА перед
  операциями с секретами, env, чувствительными данными, файлами в
  `~/.stefania/`, `~/.zshrc`**
- `~/.stefania/agent-core/references/workflows.md` — рабочие процедуры
- `~/.stefania/agent-core/references/about-product.md` — когда меня просят рассказать о себе, помочь с установкой / обновлением / доступом к моделям, спрашивают версию или что нового
- `~/.stefania/agent-core/references/skill-authoring.md` — когда создаю или улучшаю скилл, решаю стоит ли это скилла и куда его залить
- `~/.stefania/agent-core/references/kb-workflow.md` — когда читать и писать в базу знаний

Все references — в `~/.stefania/agent-core/references/`, обновляются при `/setup-stefania` и `/stefania-knowledge-base-init`.

## Доступные скиллы

Мой инструментарий — скиллы; что доступно, вижу в окружении сессии. Полный
каталог с описаниями и типовыми цепочками — `~/.stefania/agent-core/references/skills-catalog.md`:
читаю его, когда подбираю инструмент под задачу. Не вижу нужного скилла —
значит он не установлен или не настроен его токен: говорю об этом прямо,
а не изобретаю обходной путь.

## База знаний

База знаний — мой самый мощный инструмент для пользы бизнесу: она превращает
меня из универсального AI в сотрудника, который знает контекст вашей команды.
Использую её проактивно — не жду вопроса.

Можно подключить несколько именованных баз знаний. Каждая использует один из
шести режимов: Wiki, DataCatalog или read-only директория Arcadia — напрямую
либо через свой синхронизируемый Obsidian-vault. Реестр знает скилл
`stefania-knowledge-base`: обычный поиск охватывает все enabled-базы, а запись
адресуется явно или идет в default. Вопрос про дашборды /
стейкхолдеров / метрики / процессы / источники данных → первый ход всегда KB,
не Wiki/Tracker/DataLens. Перед задачей подтягиваю контекст, после — пополняю
тем, что узнала. Подробные правила — `~/.stefania/agent-core/references/kb-workflow.md`.

Если база ещё не настроена — я уже работаю: решаю задачи, веду тикеты, проверяю
качество, код-ревью и дайджесты через скиллы. Но подключи
`/stefania-knowledge-base-init` — и я буду знать метрики, процессы, заказчиков
и данные твоей команды с первого запроса, без повторных вопросов — это кратно
усиливает пользу.
<!-- stefania-core:end -->

---
name: "pdf"
description: "Read, create, inspect, render, and verify PDF files where visual layout matters, including fillable AcroForms. Use Poppler rendering plus Python tools such as reportlab, pdfplumber, and pypdf for generation and extraction."
---

# PDF Skill

## When To Use

- Read or review PDF content where layout and visuals matter.
- Create PDFs programmatically with reliable formatting.
- Fill and validate interactive PDF forms.
- Validate final rendering before delivery.

## Tools + Contract Requirements

Immediately before the first create/edit authoring command, run `mark_artifact_operation_started.mjs` successfully exactly once using the command below. Do not run it for read-only work. For edits, replace `create` with `edit`; adjust the expected count and output format to match the requested outputs.

```bash
node container_tools/mark_artifact_operation_started.mjs --operation-kind create --expected-output-count 1 --output-format pdf
```

## Workflow

1. Prefer visual review: render PDF pages to PNGs and inspect them.
   - Use `pdftoppm` from the bundled runtime or system Poppler when available.
   - If unavailable, install Poppler or ask the user to review the output locally.
2. Use `reportlab` to generate PDFs when creating new documents.
3. Use `pdfplumber` or `pypdf` for text extraction and quick checks; do not rely on text extraction for layout fidelity.
4. After each meaningful update, re-render pages and verify alignment, spacing, and legibility.

## Fill And Validate AcroForms

Visual review alone is not a correctness check for a fillable PDF. A page `/Widget` annotation can render a value from its appearance stream while the canonical `/AcroForm/Fields` tree is missing or contains a stale value.

1. Keep the result interactive by default; set `flatten=True` only when the user explicitly requests a completed, static form. Preserve the source PDF, and do not flatten a signed PDF without an explicit workflow decision.
2. Inspect both representations before filling: enumerate fields from `reader.get_fields()` and `/Widget` annotations from every page's `/Annots`, following `/Parent` and `/Kids`. If a widget and a canonical field have the same name but are distinct objects with no `/Parent` relationship, do not call `reattach_fields()` blindly: it can create a second top-level field with the same name. Report the ambiguity or produce a static result.
3. Recover genuinely orphaned widgets, fill all pages, and write the result with `pypdf`:

```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter
from pypdf.generic import NameObject

reader = PdfReader(input_pdf)
writer = PdfWriter()
writer.clone_document_from_reader(reader)

# Restores widgets that are missing from /AcroForm/Fields.
writer.reattach_fields()
fields = writer.get_fields() or {}
missing = set(expected_values) - set(fields)
if missing:
    raise ValueError(f"Form fields not found after repair: {sorted(missing)}")

values_to_write = dict(expected_values)
if flatten:
    # Paint every existing value before removing every widget.
    values_to_write = {
        name: field.get("/V", "/Off" if field.get("/FT") == "/Btn" else "")
        for name, field in fields.items()
    }
    values_to_write.update(expected_values)

writer.update_page_form_field_values(
    None, values_to_write, auto_regenerate=False, flatten=flatten
)

if flatten:
    # pypdf's flatten=True paints appearances but does not remove widgets.
    writer.remove_annotations(subtypes="/Widget")
    writer.root_object.pop(NameObject("/AcroForm"), None)

with open(output_pdf, "wb") as stream:
    writer.write(stream)
```

4. Reopen the written PDF before delivery. For an interactive result, require every expected field to be present in `get_fields()` with the expected `/V`, enumerate page widgets again, and confirm their effective `/V` (the widget value or inherited `/Parent` value) agrees. Confirm each updated widget has a non-empty `/AP` `/N` appearance and render the final pages to catch stale or clipped appearances. Do not rely on `/NeedAppearances` or a successful PNG render as proof that logical field data was updated.
5. For a flattened result, require zero `/Widget` annotations and no remaining `/AcroForm` field tree after reopening, then render the final pages. Keep an editable copy when the user may need to revise the form.

## Temp And Output Conventions

- Use `tmp/pdfs/` for intermediate files; delete them when done.
- Write final artifacts under `output/pdf/` when working in this repo.
- Keep filenames stable and descriptive.

## Dependencies

Prefer the Codex bundled workspace/runtime dependencies when available. The primary runtime is expected to include:

- Python packages: `reportlab`, `pdfplumber`, `pypdf`
- Rendering tools: `pdftoppm` and `pdfinfo` from Poppler

If a dependency is missing, install only what is needed.

Python packages:

```bash
uv pip install reportlab pdfplumber pypdf
```

If `uv` is unavailable:

```bash
python3 -m pip install reportlab pdfplumber pypdf
```

System tools for rendering:

```bash
# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install poppler

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt-get install -y poppler-utils
```

If installation is not possible in this environment, tell the user which dependency is missing and how to install it locally.

## Environment

No required environment variables.

## Rendering Command

```bash
pdftoppm -png "$INPUT_PDF" "$OUTPUT_PREFIX"
```

## Quality Expectations

- Maintain polished visual design: consistent typography, spacing, margins, and section hierarchy.
- Avoid rendering issues: clipped text, overlapping elements, broken tables, black squares, or unreadable glyphs.
- Charts, tables, and images must be sharp, aligned, and clearly labeled.
- Use ASCII hyphens only. Avoid U+2011 and other Unicode dashes.
- Citations and references must be human-readable; never leave tool tokens or placeholder strings.

## Final Checks

- Do not deliver until the latest PNG inspection shows zero visual or formatting defects.
- Confirm headers, footers, page numbering, and section transitions look polished.
- Keep intermediate files organized or remove them after final approval.

## Final response

### Final response citations

Place `:codex-file-citation{...}` inline in prose, not in a trailing list. Use `purpose="source"` for Q&A/no-op and `purpose="output"` for create/edit.

- [HARD REQUIREMENT] Create/edit: cite each final PDF exactly once with a plain output citation. Summarize representative changes; do not cite every page or add a separate filename, path, or Markdown link. Example: `Created :codex-file-citation{path="/abs/path/report.pdf" purpose="output"}, with the completed analysis and appendix.`
- Q&A/no-op: do not edit or re-export. Inspect the complete relevant pages, preserve material headings, table/figure labels, footnotes, sources, and sample sizes, and cite each source PDF once with a plain source citation.

PDF citations currently support only plain file citations. Do not add `artifact_kind`, `page_number`, or other locators. Never cite rendered PNGs, scratch files, builders, or QA intermediates unless asked.

### Final response suggested followups

- After successfully creating, editing, or analyzing an artifact, finish your final response with 3 useful next actions tailored to the artifact and the user's goal. Completing the requested work is not a reason to skip these actions: they help the user continue from the result. Do not perform the actions unless the user chooses one.
- Each action must be a distinct, concrete request the user could send next. Do not repeat completed work or invent filler. Omit the list if the user declines suggestions, the requested work fails, or no genuinely useful next action remains.
- Present each action as an unescaped Markdown list item using this exact syntax: `- :codex-followup[Short action]{prompt="Complete request for that action"}`.

Content-based Recommender Systems: State of
the Art and TrendsPasquale Lops, Marco de Gemmis and Giovanni SemeraroAbstract  Recommender systems have the effect of guiding users in a personal-
ized way to interesting objects in a large space of possible options. Content-based
recommendation systems try to recommend items similar to those a given user has
liked in the past. Indeed, the basic process performed by a content-based recom-
mender consists in matching up the attributes of a user profile in which preferences
and interests are stored, with the attributes of a content object (item), in order to
recommend to the user new interesting items. This chapter provides an overview of
content-based recommender systems, with the aim of imposing a degree of order on

L35: This chapter discusses content-based recommendation systems, i.e., systems that recommend an item to a user based upon a description of the item and a profile of the user’s interests. Content-based recommendation systems may be used in a variety of domains ranging from recommending web pages, news articles, restaurants, television programs, and items for sale.
L36: Although the details of various systems differ, content-based recommendation systems share in common a means for describing the items that may be recommended, a means for creating a profile of the user that describes the types of items the user likes, and a means of comparing items to the user profile to determine what to re commend. The profile is often created and updated automatically in response to feedback on the desirability of items that have been presented to the user.

L0: SUMMARY & USAGE LICENSE
L1: =============================================
L2: 
L3: MovieLens data sets were collected by the GroupLens Research Project
L4: at the University of Minnesota.
L5: 
L6: This data set consists of:
L7: 	* 100,000 ratings (1-5) from 943 users on 1682 movies.
L8: 	* Each user has rated at least 20 movies.
L9:         * Simple demographic info for the users (age, gender, occupation, zip)
L10: The data was collected through the MovieLens web site
L11: (movielens.umn.edu) during the seven-month period from September 19th,
L12: 1997 through April 22nd, 1998. This data has been cleaned up - users
L13: who had less than 20 ratings or did not have complete demographic
L14: information were removed from this data set. Detailed descriptions of
L15: the data file can be found at the end of this file.

L61: FURTHER INFORMATION ABOUT THE GROUPLENS RESEARCH PROJECT
L62: ==============================================
L63: The GroupLens Research Project is a research group in the Department
L64: of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Minnesota.
L65: Members of the GroupLens Research Project are involved in many
L66: research projects related to the fields of information filtering,
L67: collaborative filtering, and recommender systems. The project is lead
L68: by professors John Riedl and Joseph Konstan. The project began to
L69: explore automated collaborative filtering in 1992, but is most well
L70: known for its world wide trial of an automated collaborative filtering
L71: system for Usenet news in 1996.  The technology developed in the
L72: Usenet trial formed the base for the formation of Net Perceptions,
L73: Inc., which was founded by members of GroupLens Research. Since then
L74: the project has expanded its scope to research overall information
L75: filtering solutions, integrating in content-based methods as well as
L76: improving current collaborative filtering technology.
L77: Further information on the GroupLens Research project, including
L78: research publications, can be found at the following web site:
L79: 
L80:         http://www.grouplens.org/
L81: 
L82: GroupLens Research currently operates a movie recommender based on
L83: collaborative filtering:
L84: 
L85:         http://www.movielens.org/
L86: 
L87: DETAILED DESCRIPTIONS OF DATA FILES
L88: ==============================================
L89: 
L90: Here are brief descriptions of the data.
L91: ml-data.tar.gz   -- Compressed tar file.  To rebuild the u data files do this:
L92:                 gunzip ml-data.tar.gz
L93:                 tar xvf ml-data.tar
L94:                 mku.sh
L95: u.data     -- The full u data set, 100000 ratings by 943 users on 1682 items.
L96:               Each user has rated at least 20 movies.  Users and items are
L97:               numbered consecutively from 1.  The data is randomly
L98:               ordered. This is a tab separated list of
L99: 	         user id | item id | rating | timestamp.
L100:               The time stamps are unix seconds since 1/1/1970 UTC
L101: 
L102: u.info     -- The number of users, items, and ratings in the u data set.
L103: u.item     -- Information about the items (movies); this is a tab separated
L104:               list of
L105:               movie id | movie title | release date | video release date |
L106:               IMDb URL | unknown | Action | Adventure | Animation |
L107:               Children's | Comedy | Crime | Documentary | Drama | Fantasy |
L108:               Film-Noir | Horror | Musical | Mystery | Romance | Sci-Fi |
L109:               Thriller | War | Western |
L110:               The last 19 fields are the genres, a 1 indicates the movie
L111:               is of that genre, a 0 indicates it is not; movies can be in
L112:               several genres at once.
L113:               The movie ids are the ones used in the u.data data set.
L114: u.genre    -- A list of the genres.
L115: 
L116: u.user     -- Demographic information about the users; this is a tab
L117:               separated list of
L118:               user id | age | gender | occupation | zip code

L128: u4.base
L129: u4.test
L130: u5.base
L131: u5.test
L132: ua.base    -- The data sets ua.base, ua.test, ub.base, and ub.test
L133: ua.test       split the u data into a training set and a test set with
L134: ub.base       exactly 10 ratings per user in the test set.  The sets
L135: ub.test       ua.test and ub.test are disjoint.  These data sets can
L136:               be generated from u.data by mku.sh.
L137: 
L138: allbut.pl  -- The script that generates training and test sets where
L139:               all but n of a users ratings are in the training data.
L140: mku.sh     -- A shell script to generate all the u data sets from u.data.

L33:   * 11 cite14†Altmetric†link.altmetric.com L34: ## Abstract
L35: Recommender systems have the effect of guiding users in a personalized way to interesting objects in a large space of possible options. Content-based recommendation systems try to recommend items similar to those a given user has liked in the past.
L36: Indeed, the basic process performed by a content-based recommender consists in matching up the attributes of a user profile in which preferences and interests are stored, with the attributes of a content object (item), in order to recommend to the user new interesting items. This chapter provides an overview of content-based recommender systems, with the aim of imposing a degree of order on the diversity of the different aspects involved in their design and implementation.
L37: The first part of the chapter presents the basic concepts and terminology of contentbased recommender systems, a high level architecture, and their main advantages and drawbacks. The second part of the chapter provides a review of the state of the art of systems adopted in several application domains, by thoroughly describing both classical and advanced techniques for representing items and user profiles. The most widely adopted techniques for learning user profiles are also presented.
L38: The last part of the chapter discusses trends and future research which might lead towards the next generation of systems, by describing the role of User Generated Content as a way for taking into account evolving vocabularies, and the challenge of feeding users with serendipitous recommendations, that is to say surprisingly interesting items that they might not have otherwise discovered.

From a Single Movie to a User Profile: A Reproducible
Content-Based Movie Recommender
Student: Ivan Tsarikov
Team: Individual
Assignment: A02 - Content-Based Filtering (Week 2)
Date: 2026-09-22
Abstract - Content-based movie recommendation can fail when genre metadata is parsed incorrectly and a single active title is
treated as the user's whole preference. This study repairs the MovieLens 100K baseline, averages three 19-dimensional genre
vectors, ranks unseen films by cosine similarity, and uses Bayesian rating quality only for ties. Across 942 eligible users,
item-to-item and profile-based Top-5 lists overlapped by 0.89 titles (17.9%), while cosine expanded profile coverage from 11.7%
under raw overlap to 20.5%. The results support combining stable profiles with item-level retrieval and explicit novelty controls.
Index Terms - content-based recommendation, cosine similarity, user profiles, MovieLens, catalog discovery
1. Introduction
The original Week 2 application recommended movies from one selected title using broad genre labels. Its implementation also mapped
19 MovieLens genre flags onto only 18 names, shifting every known genre and discarding the final Western flag. The resulting interface
could return semantically wrong or zero-overlap titles.
The practical goal was to preserve the starter application's simple web interface while making the model correct, explainable, and more
representative of a user's taste. For example, a viewer who selected Toy Story, GoldenEye, and Four Rooms should receive an
aggregate profile rather than a list determined by only one of those titles.
Contributions.
 - Corrected all 19 genre positions, added strict parsing, deterministic ranking, watched-item exclusion, and executable tests.
 - Replaced naive single-item matching with cosine similarity over an averaged three-movie profile and evaluated relevance, bias, and
 discovery behavior.
2. Related Work
Content-based systems represent items with attributes, construct a user-interest profile, and compare candidates with that profile [3].
Lops, de Gemmis, and Semeraro describe this profile-to-item matching pattern and identify limited content, overspecialization, and
serendipity as central concerns [4]. MovieLens supplies a stable, documented benchmark for reproducible recommendation studies [1],
[2].
Alternatives considered. Jaccard similarity was transparent but ignored preference frequency in the averaged profile. Raw dot product
preserved weights but favored movies carrying many genre flags. Collaborative filtering could use rating interactions, but it would change
the assignment from a content baseline and introduce cold-start behavior; ratings were therefore restricted to deterministic tie-breaking.
The implementation follows the web Fetch specification for asynchronous data loading [5] and otherwise uses no production libraries.


===== PAGE 2 =====

Page 2
3. Method
Each movie is a binary vector over the 19 MovieLens genres in the documented order from Unknown through Western [2]. The profile is
the component-wise mean of three distinct watched movies. Every unseen candidate receives cosine similarity to that profile; scores of
zero are removed and the five highest scores are retained.

If either vector has zero magnitude, similarity is defined as 0. Candidates are ordered by cosine score, then Bayesian-smoothed rating
quality, rating count, title, and movie ID. The quality tie-breaker is:

The prior weight of 50 prevents a movie with one unusually high rating from winning a tie over a well-supported title. It does not convert

Abstract - Content-based movie recommendation can fail when genre metadata is parsed incorrectly and a single active title is
treated as the user's whole preference. This study repairs the MovieLens 100K baseline, averages three 19-dimensional genre
vectors, ranks unseen films by cosine similarity, and uses Bayesian rating quality only for ties. Across 942 eligible users,
item-to-item and profile-based Top-5 lists overlapped by 0.89 titles (17.9%), while cosine expanded profile coverage from 11.7%
under raw overlap to 20.5%. The results support combining stable profiles with item-level retrieval and explicit novelty controls.
Index Terms - content-based recommendation, cosine similarity, user profiles, MovieLens, catalog discovery
1. Introduction
The original Week 2 application recommended movies from one selected title using broad genre labels. Its implementation also mapped
19 MovieLens genre flags onto only 18 names, shifting every known genre and discarding the final Western flag. The resulting interface
could return semantically wrong or zero-overlap titles.
The practical goal was to preserve the starter application's simple web interface while making the model correct, explainable, and more
representative of a user's taste. For example, a viewer who selected Toy Story, GoldenEye, and Four Rooms should receive an
aggregate profile rather than a list determined by only one of those titles.
Contributions.
 - Corrected all 19 genre positions, added strict parsing, deterministic ranking, watched-item exclusion, and executable tests.
 - Replaced naive single-item matching with cosine similarity over an averaged three-movie profile and evaluated relevance, bias, and
 discovery behavior.
2. Related Work
Content-based systems represent items with attributes, construct a user-interest profile, and compare candidates with that profile [3].
Lops, de Gemmis, and Semeraro describe this profile-to-item matching pattern and identify limited content, overspecialization, and
serendipity as central concerns [4]. MovieLens supplies a stable, documented benchmark for reproducible recommendation studies [1],
[2].
Alternatives considered. Jaccard similarity was transparent but ignored preference frequency in the averaged profile. Raw dot product
preserved weights but favored movies carrying many genre flags. Collaborative filtering could use rating interactions, but it would change
the assignment from a content baseline and introduce cold-start behavior; ratings were therefore restricted to deterministic tie-breaking.
The implementation follows the web Fetch specification for asynchronous data loading [5] and otherwise uses no production libraries.

3. Method
Each movie is a binary vector over the 19 MovieLens genres in the documented order from Unknown through Western [2]. The profile is
the component-wise mean of three distinct watched movies. Every unseen candidate receives cosine similarity to that profile; scores of
zero are removed and the five highest scores are retained.

Figure 1. Production recommendation pipeline. Ratings never change the cosine score; they only resolve exact ties.
 profile = (v1 + v2 + v3) / 3
 cosine(P, C) = (P dot C) / (norm(P) x norm(C))
If either vector has zero magnitude, similarity is defined as 0. Candidates are ordered by cosine score, then Bayesian-smoothed rating
quality, rating count, title, and movie ID. The quality tie-breaker is:
 quality(i) = n_i/(n_i + 50) x mean_i + 50/(n_i + 50) x global_mean
The prior weight of 50 prevents a movie with one unusually high rating from winning a tie over a well-supported title. It does not convert
the method into collaborative filtering because rating data is not part of the content score.
